prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation by heterobifunctional small molecules that bring a target protein and an E3 ubiquitin ligase together

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is the kind of game-changer I look for: a completely new idea (degrade a protein by induced proximity instead of inhibiting it) that is chemically simple, and has already had real consequences. Three members ranked it first and four placed it in their top three, and the support is broad rather than a single enthusiast's. Crews and Deshaies conceived and demonstrated the PROTAC concept. Ciulli's VHL ligands and his structural and ternary-complex work turned it into rational, quantitative design, which is the connection between mechanism and experiment that I value. The idea has been reproduced across many laboratories and targets and has reached late-stage clinical trials, so the consequences are no longer hypothetical. The three-name trio is a clean PROTAC prize that stays inside the three-laureate limit.
statement.case_against: No PROTAC has yet been approved, and Brzezinski and Somfai are right that clinical validation is still incomplete. The attribution is also crowded: the cereblon and thalidomide molecular-glue strand (Handa, Ito, and the Gray and Sakamoto contributions) is arguably a separate discovery, and a PROTAC-only trio leaves out the people who explained why thalidomide works. Sakamoto's early first PROTAC with Crews and Deshaies is a further priority claim I cannot fully settle from the supplied credits.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranked targeted protein degradation only seventh because several PROTACs are in late-stage trials but none is approved, and put electron transfer through proteins (B055) and nitrogenase (B046) first and second on grounds of mechanistic depth and long confirmation.
responses.response: I take the point on approval seriously, but the Nobel standard is a new concept with demonstrated consequences, not a marketed drug. The mechanistic principles are confirmed by structures and cell biology in many independent labs, so this is not the situation of an unconfirmed claim. I respect Gray and Winkler's work: it is exactly the quantitative physical chemistry I like. Yet it extends Marcus theory, which was already honored, whereas degradation is a new modality. On nitrogenase I agree the structures are solid, but you yourself note that the central N2 reduction mechanism is still debated, which makes that prize less complete than this one.

responses.point: Aili ranked B019 first but would credit Crews, Deshaies and Handa, arguing that Handa's identification of cereblon as the thalidomide target underpins the molecular-glue arm and the clinical IMiD story.
responses.response: We agree on the prize, and I accept that Handa's cereblon work is a real discovery of high importance. My disagreement is on what the citation is about. If the citation is rational design of bifunctional degraders, Ciulli's VHL ligands and structure-guided work are intrinsic to it, whereas Handa's discovery explains a drug that was already in clinical use. Putting Handa in would turn it into a two-strand prize that is harder to articulate in one sentence. I would keep Handa as the strongest argument for a second prize part if the committee insists on covering the glue strand, but I do not think it is needed.

responses.point: Linke ranked nanopore sequencing (B002) first for a clear physical principle turned into label-free long-read sequencing, and ranked degradation fourth because the biophysics of ternary complex cooperativity is still not fully worked out and approvals are missing.
responses.response: I agree that nanopore sensing is mature and well confirmed, and I list it as an alternative. My reservations are attribution: Linke himself says credit is spread over more than three people, and Kasianowicz, Branton, Deamer, Bayley and Akeson all have defensible claims. A prize that must exclude two of five is hard to defend, and Bayley is conspicuously absent from your trio. On ternary complex cooperativity, I would say it is the active mechanistic frontier and this is where Ciulli's work is strongest, which is another argument for naming him rather than a reason to wait.

responses.point: Somfai put Buchwald and Hartwig's Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first on grounds of three decades of use and stable mechanism, and ranked degradation fourth since no PROTAC degrader is approved yet.
responses.response: The amination is an excellent and clean two-person candidate and I would not oppose it, but the 2010 cross-coupling prize already covers the central conceptual territory of palladium catalysis and this one is an important extension rather than a new idea. By my 'game-changer' standard I prefer the modality that opens a new area of pharmacology. I accept your clinical-approval caution; I would weigh it less because the committee has not required an approved product before, and the evidence for the principle is far beyond a single group.

uncertainties: Whether the molecular-glue and cereblon strand (Handa, Ito) should be a separate prize part, or whether Sakamoto should be credited with the first PROTAC alongside Crews and Deshaies.
Whether the committee will accept that the absence of an approved PROTAC drug is not an obstacle.
Whether base editing (B043) is a stronger and more timely candidate once the Kondo and Nishida priority question is settled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B019, B043 or B002. My connections (Warshel, Uppsala ribosome and RNA community, long service with Brzezinski) do not touch the people named, and I do not collaborate with the credited candidates.
